section.title: Oholah and Oholibah
section.sectionRationale: This is Ezekiel's second, even more explicit allegory of two sisters, Oholah, Samaria, and Oholibah, Jerusalem, whose names play on the Hebrew word for tent, marking the city where God's own tent, the temple, truly stood as the more culpable of the two. Their shared history of political and religious 'prostitution,' pursuing alliances with Assyria and Babylon as spiritual adultery against the LORD, is confronted with the same shocking honesty as chapter 16, handled with the same pastoral care: acknowledged plainly, never treated as entertainment, and never separated from the reality of God's own grief and righteous jealousy.
section.thesis: Two sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem, are exposed as having pursued the very political and religious alliances they should have refused, Jerusalem's betrayal graver still because God's own dwelling stood within her walls, and both are judged by the very nations they once desired, a devastating picture of covenant unfaithfulness that finds its full and final answer only in Christ, the faithful Bridegroom who does not abandon His unfaithful people but cleanses and presents His church spotless.
section.frameNote: Six movements: two sisters introduced, and the elder, Oholah, falls to her lovers the Assyrians; the younger, Oholibah, proves even more depraved, adding Babylon to her pursuits; judgment announced as her own former lovers turn destroyers; a shared cup of judgment drained down to its dregs; shared abominations including child sacrifice and a defiled sanctuary; and the sentence finally executed, ending this indecency as a warning to all.

units.label: Two sisters, and the elder's fall to Assyria

verses.text: Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, there were two women, daughters of the same mother,
and they played in Egypt, prostituting themselves from their youth. Their breasts were fondled there, and their virgin bosoms caressed.

The older was named {{oholah_oholibah|Oholah}}, and her sister was named {{oholah_oholibah|Oholibah}}. They became Mine and gave birth to sons and daughters. As for their identities, Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem.
Oholah {{zanah|prostituted}} herself while she was still Mine. She lusted after her lovers, the Assyrians, warriors
clothed in blue, governors and commanders, all desirable young men, horsemen mounted on steeds.
She offered sexual favors to all the elite of Assyria. She defiled herself with all the idols of those for whom she lusted.
She did not give up the prostitution she began in Egypt, when men slept with her in her youth, caressed her virgin bosom, and poured out their lust upon her.
Therefore I delivered her into the hands of her lovers, the Assyrians for whom she lusted.
They exposed her nakedness, seized her sons and daughters, and put her to the sword. Thus she became a byword among women, and they executed judgment against her.
Her sister Oholibah saw this, yet in her lust and prostitution she was more depraved than her sister.
She too lusted after the Assyrians, governors and commanders, warriors dressed in splendor, horsemen riding on steeds, all desirable young men.
And I saw that she too had defiled herself; both of them had taken the same path.
But Oholibah carried her prostitution even further. She saw the men portrayed on the wall, images of the Chaldeans, engraved in vermilion,
wearing belts on their waists and flowing turbans on their heads; all of them looked like officers of the Babylonians in Chaldea, the land of their birth.
At the sight of them, she lusted for them and sent messengers to them in Chaldea.
Then the Babylonians came to her, to the bed of love, and in their lust they defiled her. But after she had been defiled by them, she turned away in disgust.
When Oholibah openly prostituted herself and exposed her nakedness, I turned away from her in disgust, just as I had turned away from her sister.
Yet she multiplied her promiscuity, remembering the days of her youth, when she had prostituted herself in the land of Egypt
and lusted after their lovers, whose genitals were like those of donkeys and whose emission was like that of stallions.
So you revisited the indecency of your youth, when the Egyptians caressed your bosom and pressed your young breasts.

units.label: Judgment: her own lovers turn against her
units.note: the very nations she pursued become her destroyers

verses.text: Therefore, Oholibah, this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I will incite your lovers against you, those from whom you turned away in disgust. And I will bring them against you from every side,

the Babylonians and all the Chaldeans, the men of Pekod, Shoa, and Koa, and all the Assyrians with them, all desirable young men, governors and commanders, officers and men of renown, mounted on horses.

They will come against you with a host of peoples, with weapons, chariots, and wagons. They will array themselves against you on every side with buckler and shield and helmet. I will delegate judgment to them, and they will punish you according to their own standards.

And I will set My {{qinah|jealous rage}} against you, and they will deal with you in fury. They will cut off your noses and ears, and your survivors will fall by the sword. They will seize your sons and daughters, and your remnant will be consumed by fire.
They will strip off your clothes and take your fine jewelry.
So I will put an end to your indecency and prostitution, which began in the land of Egypt, and you will not lift your eyes to them or remember Egypt anymore.’
For this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Surely I will deliver you into the hands of those you hate, from whom you turned away in disgust.
They will treat you with hatred, take all for which you have worked, and leave you naked and bare, so that the shame of your prostitution will be exposed. Your indecency and promiscuity
have brought these things upon you, because you have prostituted yourself with the nations and defiled yourself with their idols.

units.label: Her sister's cup, drained to the dregs

verses.text: Because you have followed the path of your sister, I will put her cup into your hand.’
This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘You will drink your sister's {{kos|cup}}, a cup deep and wide. It will bring scorn and derision, for it holds so much.
You will be filled with drunkenness and grief, with a cup of devastation and desolation, the cup of your sister Samaria.
You will drink it and drain it; you will dash it to pieces, and tear your breasts. For I have spoken,’ declares the Lord GOD.
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Because you have forgotten Me and have cast Me behind your back, you must bear the consequences of your indecency and prostitution.’”

units.label: Shared abominations: child sacrifice and a defiled sanctuary
units.note: the same day they slaughtered children, they entered My sanctuary

verses.text: Then the LORD said to me: “Son of man, will you pass judgment against Oholah and Oholibah? Then declare to them their abominations.

For they have committed adultery, and blood is on their hands. They have committed adultery with their idols. They have even sacrificed their children, whom they bore to Me, in the fire as food for their idols.
They have also done this to Me: On that very same day, they defiled My sanctuary and profaned My Sabbaths.
On the very day they slaughtered their children for their idols, they entered My sanctuary to profane it. Yes, they did this inside My house.
Furthermore, you sisters sent messengers for men who came from afar; and behold, when they arrived, you bathed for them, painted your eyes, and adorned yourself with jewelry.
You sat on a couch of luxury with a table spread before it, on which you had set My incense and My oil,
accompanied by the sound of a carefree crowd. Drunkards were brought in from the desert along with men from the rabble, who put bracelets on your wrists and beautiful crowns on your head.

units.label: The sentence executed; indecency ended in the land
units.note: a warning to every woman not to imitate this behavior

verses.text: Then I said of her who had grown old in adulteries: ‘Now let them use her as a prostitute, for that is all she is!’
And they slept with her as with a prostitute; they slept with Oholah and Oholibah, those lewd women.
But righteous men will sentence them to the punishment of those who commit adultery and bloodshed, because they are adulteresses with blood on their hands.
This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Bring a mob against them and consign them to terror and plunder.
The mob will stone them and cut them down with their swords. They will kill their sons and daughters and burn down their houses.
So I will put an end to indecency in the land, and all the women will be admonished not to imitate your behavior.
They will repay you for your indecency, and you will bear the consequences of your sins of idolatry. Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.’”

oholah_oholibah.gloss: Her tent / My tent is in her. Samaria's name means simply 'her own tent,' a shrine of her own making, while Jerusalem's name, 'my tent is in her,' marks her as the city where God's true tent, the temple, actually stood, a wordplay explaining why Jerusalem's betrayal, described as surpassing her sister's, verse 11, is judged so much more severely: greater privilege bore greater responsibility.

zanah.gloss: To act as a prostitute, to be sexually unfaithful. Used throughout this chapter, and its sister-chapter 16, as the primary metaphor for covenant idolatry, Israel and Judah's pursuit of foreign gods and foreign alliances pictured as marital betrayal of the LORD.

qinah.gloss: Jealousy or jealous rage, the passionate response of a betrayed covenant partner rather than cold cruelty. God's qinah against Oholibah reflects the same relational anguish behind the marriage language of the whole chapter, wounded love responding to betrayal, not indifferent wrath.

kos.gloss: Cup, here specifically a cup of divine wrath, deep and wide, that Jerusalem must drink after her sister Samaria. This image of judgment's inescapable, shared consequence recurs throughout the prophets, Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15-29, and reappears in Revelation 14:10.

basic.context: This is Ezekiel's second, even more graphic allegory of covenant unfaithfulness, picturing Samaria and Jerusalem as two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, whose very names, playing on the Hebrew word for tent, mark Jerusalem's betrayal as the graver of the two, since God's own tent, the temple, actually stood within her. Both sisters pursue the political and military powers of their day, Assyria and then Babylon, as illicit lovers, and both are ultimately destroyed by the very powers they once desired, ending in a stark warning against every future repetition of this behavior.
basic.hermeneutics: As with chapter 16, this is deliberately shocking allegory, using the ancient Near Eastern language of marital infidelity to expose the seriousness of political and religious alliance-seeking as spiritual adultery against the LORD. Its graphic imagery should be read with the same pastoral honesty as its sister chapter, acknowledged plainly for what it communicates about sin's true nature, never sanitized into vagueness nor lingered over for its own sake.
basic.originalLanguages: Oholah, 'her own tent,' and Oholibah, 'my tent is in her,' name Samaria and Jerusalem respectively, the wordplay itself explaining why Jerusalem's zanah, prostitution, described as exceeding her sister's, is judged more severely: greater nearness to God's true dwelling meant greater accountability. Judgment falls as God's own qinah, jealous rage, and as a shared kos, cup, of wrath both sisters must drain.
basic.typology: Jerusalem's judgment for defiling the very sanctuary where God's tent stood contrasts sharply with the New Testament's picture of the church as God's true and lasting temple, and Jerusalem's serial unfaithfulness as a bride, despite unique privilege, is answered by Christ's unwavering faithfulness to His own bride, the church, whom He cleanses and presents to Himself without spot or blemish.
basic.christ: Where Oholibah, privileged above her sister by God's own dwelling among her, proves even more unfaithful, the New Testament presents Christ as the Bridegroom who, though His bride has every advantage of nearness to Him, remains faithful even when she does not, loving the church and giving Himself up for her so that He might sanctify her and present her to Himself in splendor, Ephesians 5:25-27, succeeding perfectly where Jerusalem, and every human heart, repeatedly fails.
basic.god: God's anger in this chapter is the anger of betrayed, covenant love, not cold cruelty; He describes His own reaction in strikingly personal terms, disgust, jealousy, grief, showing that idolatry wounds Him relationally, not merely violates an abstract rule. Yet even this severe chapter's warning, that such indecency will finally end, carries within it God's ultimate purpose that His people would live in a way that reflects, rather than betrays, His holiness.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 3:6-11 similarly compares Israel and Judah as two unfaithful sisters, with Judah judged more severely for having seen her sister's judgment and remaining unrepentant still. Hosea 1-3 tells a parallel story of covenant infidelity and pursuing love. Ephesians 5:25-27 describes Christ's sanctifying, cleansing love for His bride, the church, in deliberate contrast to this chapter's picture of betrayal. Revelation 17-19 contrasts the great prostitute Babylon with the pure bride, the New Jerusalem, adorned for her husband.
basic.oneStory: This is the story of two sisters whose privileged nearness to God became the very measure of their unfaithfulness, judged at last by the very powers they had pursued as lovers. Yet the God who describes His own grief and jealousy so personally in this chapter is the same God who, in Christ, remains faithful to an unfaithful bride, cleansing and presenting her to Himself in splendor, succeeding everywhere Oholah and Oholibah failed.

context.literary:
The chapter is a story told in three settings and then retold as a verdict. Verses 1 to 10 give the older sister's career in a few strokes, from Egypt to Assyria to execution. Verses 11 to 21 slow down for the younger, adding a second lover, Babylon, whom she summons by messenger after seeing painted figures on a wall. Verses 22 to 35 turn the lovers into the court: the men she courted come against her, and the sister's cup is placed in her hand. Verses 36 to 49 go back to the charge sheet and add the sins of worship, then close with the sentence executed and a lesson for 'all the women.'

Three repeated devices carry the argument. The first is the sight-then-lust sequence. Oholibah sees, desires, sends, and is defiled, verses 14 to 17, and the motion from eye to messenger to bed is the motion of foreign policy told as seduction. The second is the cycle of disgust. Her soul is wrenched away from her lovers, verse 17, and God's soul is wrenched away from her, verse 18, using the same verb, so that her faithlessness is mirrored in His withdrawal. The third is the doubling of the sisters' fate. 'Both of them had taken the same path,' verse 13, and she drinks 'your sister's cup,' verse 32, tying Jerusalem's end to Samaria's as a deliberate lesson.

The chapter is the pair to Ezekiel 16, which tells the history of one woman from foundling to bride to harlot. Chapter 23 divides her in two and adds the politics. Where 16 stresses grace received and spurned, 23 stresses alliance after alliance, and the Egyptian youth in verse 3 recalls what Ezekiel had said in 20:7 to 8.
context.historical:
Behind the allegory lies nearly two centuries of diplomacy. Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom, sought Assyrian help early, as when Menahem paid Pul a thousand talents of silver, 2 Kings 15:19 to 20, and later played with Egypt against Assyria, 2 Kings 17:4. In 722 BC Assyria took the city and deported its people. Ezekiel's 'put her to the sword' is the memory of that disaster.

Judah did the same in its own way. Ahaz appealed to Tiglath-pileser, and on a visit to Damascus he saw a foreign altar and had a copy made for the Temple, 2 Kings 16:10 to 11. This is the 'defiling herself with all the idols' of the Assyrians, verse 7, in a literal sense. Hezekiah received envoys from Babylon and showed them his treasuries and armory, 2 Kings 20:12 to 13, an early instance of the courting that verse 16 describes. When Babylon came to power, Judah's kings alternately submitted to and plotted against it, finally turning again to Egypt, Ezekiel 17:15.

The wall paintings of verse 14 are plausible. Chaldean officers appear in the text as figures drawn in red ochre, shashar, a pigment also used in Jeremiah 22:14 for a house's paint. Whether Ezekiel means actual reliefs seen by Judean envoys or a figure of fascination, the effect is that Jerusalem's leaders were dazzled by the imperial power's image before they met the power itself.

The names in verse 23, Pekod, Shoa and Koa, are usually taken to be peoples east of the Tigris, subject to Babylon, so the army that comes is a multinational host. And when verse 25 speaks of noses and ears cut off, it describes the sort of mutilation of captives practised in the ancient Near East. The women of verse 48 are not a separate group but the whole audience, since the allegory is told by a prophet to a mixed community of men and women.
context.canonical:
The sisters are not an isolated image. Hosea had already married a woman who would be unfaithful, Hosea 1:2 and 3:1, to preach the same word. Jeremiah 3:6 to 11 put two sisters, faithless Israel and unfaithful Judah, in the same frame, and said that Judah saw Israel's divorce and was unmoved, so that Israel came off looking 'more righteous.' Ezekiel 16:51 to 52 says the same of Samaria and Sodom. Chapter 23 gives the idea its most violent expression.

The 'cup' of verses 31 to 34 is among the biggest images in the prophets. The Lord holds a cup of wrath that nations must drink, Psalm 75:8, and Jeremiah is told to make the nations drink it, Jeremiah 25:15. Isaiah says Jerusalem has drained it to the dregs, Isaiah 51:17, while Lamentations 4:21 and Habakkuk 2:16 say it will pass to others. In the Gospels Jesus asks that the cup pass from Him, 'Yet not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39.

The marriage frame also carries forward. Paul can say he betrothed the church to one husband, 2 Corinthians 11:2, and Ephesians 5:25 to 27 uses the same idea in the other direction, with the husband cleansing and presenting his bride. Revelation sets two women side by side. One is the great prostitute with her golden cup, Babylon, Revelation 17:1 to 5, and the other is the bride of the Lamb in fine linen, Revelation 19:7 to 8. Ezekiel 23 is the Old Testament source of both pictures.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel's purpose is to rob the exiles of an excuse. They knew their kings had made treaties and that the kings had counted themselves clever. The allegory says that every treaty with an empire was also a worship, because to ally with a power in the ancient world meant adopting its gods, its altars and its protection. Politics and religion were one act. To feel that one was merely managing a crisis was precisely the self-deception being exposed.

The chapter also meant to prevent the Judeans from drawing the wrong lesson from Samaria. Samaria's fall might have confirmed their sense of being the better sister. Instead Oholibah 'saw this, yet' went further, verse 11. Seeing a neighbour's ruin and not turning is the aggravating factor. The oracle is a warning that the generation which watched Samaria fall has less excuse, not more.

The sharpest purpose is to show how God experiences betrayal. The verbs of the chapter are those of a wounded person: disgust, jealousy, turning away. He is not a distant lawgiver whose statutes were broken. He was a husband whose house was used, verses 38 and 39. The allegory was shocking because the offence was personal. And the closing instruction that 'all the women will be admonished,' verse 48, shows that the aim was reform, not mere reporting, so that those who survive might not repeat it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes sin in language that is deliberately raw, and the language is not for imitation. Ezekiel is not endorsing the culture's way of speaking about women or sex. He is using a shocking metaphor within its own world to say something about the seriousness of covenant betrayal. Readers should be careful to attend to the point and not linger over the detail.

The violence of the sentence, mutilation, burning and stoning, is likewise a record of what Judah's world did to conquered cities and to condemned adulteresses under the law, Leviticus 20:10. It is not an instruction to Christians to inflict such penalties. The New Testament places judgment in God's hands, Romans 12:19, and Jesus' handling of the woman caught in adultery, John 8:3 to 11, shows that mercy and truth come together in Him.

What does carry forward is the warning against spiritual adultery. James 4:4 uses the same language of the friendship with the world that makes one an enemy of God, and John closes his first letter, 'keep yourselves from idols,' 1 John 5:21. The chapter is also a caution against alliances that compromise worship, whether those are political, cultural or personal. And for those who have been wronged in marriage or abused, the chapter is not a model for how to speak of them: the speaker here is the offended covenant Lord, and the language is shaped around the people who committed the offence, not around victims.

debates.question: Why does the allegory begin in Egypt, verse 3, when other prophets treat Egypt as the place of rescue?

views.label: Ezekiel's own reading of Israel's history
views.case: Ezekiel 20:7 to 8 says Israel carried Egypt's idols and refused to leave them, even in Egypt. On this reading chapter 23 is consistent with the rest of the book: the habit of worshipping what the nations worship goes back to the beginning, and the exodus rescued a people who were already compromised.

views.label: A rhetorical device to mark continuity of character
views.case: The Egyptian youth is not a claim of a literal era of idolatry, but a way of saying that Israel's nature did not change. Hosea 2:15 and Jeremiah 2:2 remember the early days as devoted, so the pictures differ in purpose and not in contradiction.

views.label: A deliberate reversal of the exodus story
views.case: By placing the sisters' first lovers in Egypt, the oracle lets the Egyptians and later powers be one chain. The people who were pulled out of Egypt run back to Egypt's habits, and in the end to Egypt itself, as verses 19 to 21 imply.

debates.bearing: The simplest reading takes the chapter at its own word: the book has already said that Israel's idolatry began there, and this is the same claim in allegory. The other views do not conflict, since Hosea and Jeremiah describe devotion that was real in the wilderness while Ezekiel describes what lay under it.

debates.question: How should the sexual imagery be handled in teaching and reading?

views.label: Read it plainly and with restraint
views.case: The shock is intentional, and skipping it would hide the point that sin is a betrayal of love and not a mere rule break. Teachers should name what the text is doing and then move quickly to its meaning, especially with mixed audiences and with those who have suffered abuse.

views.label: Treat it as a problem the text itself creates
views.case: Some modern readers argue that making a woman the image of sin, and then having her punished by violence, can reinforce harm toward women. They say interpreters should say so aloud and not defend it.

views.label: Notice that the shock lands on men
views.case: Others note that the sisters stand for whole peoples including their male leaders, and that the original audience, mostly men, was being asked to see themselves as the wife. On that reading the metaphor works against male self-confidence, not for it.

debates.bearing: The second and third views both have a point. The text is a prophetic indictment in the voice of a wronged husband, and it asks for care. A faithful reading does not minimise the images and does not turn them into a lesson about women. It keeps the focus on the people's treachery and on the God who was personally wounded.

study.originalLanguages:
The two names are built on the word for tent, ohel. Oholah is 'her tent' and Oholibah is 'my tent is in her,' and the difference between them is the whole argument. A tent can be the shrine of a foreign god, a place of her own, or the place where the Lord dwells. The older sister's name says she has her own place of worship, the younger's that God's own dwelling stands inside her. That is why the greater privilege lends greater guilt.

The main verb of desire in the chapter is agab, 'to lust' or 'dote on,' which recurs through verses 5, 7, 9, 12, 16 and 20. Jeremiah 4:30 uses a related form of the word for lovers who despise the woman who adorned herself for them. The word is fitted to a relationship built on appearance and use. It names the lust of the eye that Ezekiel connects with the Assyrian and Babylonian figures on the wall.

Verses 17 and 18 use a verb, yaqa', which means to be wrenched or torn away, and it is used of Oholibah's soul pulling away from the Babylonians and then, repeatedly, of God's soul being wrenched from her. Jeremiah 6:8 uses the same verb of the Lord's own soul in warning. The repetition makes the point that betrayal damages both sides, and that God is not merely a spectator of her misery.

The vocabulary of nakedness, ervah, in verses 10, 18 and 29 is the vocabulary of Leviticus 18, where the same word is in the repeated phrase 'uncover the nakedness.' Ezekiel is deliberately using the law's own term. The exposure that the lovers inflict is a reversal of the covenant: the one who was meant to be covered by God is laid bare by those she courted.

The word for 'mob,' qahal, in verses 46 and 47 is the same noun used for the assembly of Israel. The community that should have gathered to worship gathers to carry out the sentence, as in Ezekiel 16:40. Qahal is also the word the Greek Old Testament renders ekklesia, the word the New Testament uses for the church, though that later usage is not in view here.

Finally, the 'cup' of verses 31 to 34 is described as 'deep and wide.' The cup, kos, is a measure of what has to be swallowed, and Ezekiel expands it beyond any normal vessel. The prophets use the same word for a divine portion of either blessing or judgment, as in Psalm 16:5 and Psalm 75:8, and the choice of the word makes the sentence a portion handed out by God's own hand.

typology.type: The tent, God's dwelling, and the one who 'tabernacled'
typology.fulfillment: Oholibah's name reminds Judah that God's tent stood in her. John 1:14 says the Word became flesh and 'dwelt among us,' using the verb that means to pitch a tent, so that Jesus is the true dwelling of God among men. The escalation is that God no longer sits in a building the people can defile, as in verses 38 and 39, but in a person who cannot be defiled. Paul then says believers are being built into 'a dwelling place for God in His Spirit,' Ephesians 2:22, and also speaks of the body as a temple, 1 Corinthians 6:19. The type falls short since a building could be profaned, while the Lord's presence in Christ and His people is secured by His own faithfulness.

typology.type: The bride who betrays and the Bridegroom who stays
typology.fulfillment: The marriage frame runs through the prophets. Hosea says the Lord will betroth His people in righteousness, justice, love and compassion, and faithfulness, Hosea 2:19 to 20. In the New Testament Christ is the husband who loved the church and gave Himself for her, cleansing her and presenting her radiant, Ephesians 5:25 to 27. The two sisters, who could not keep faith even with a faithful husband, become in Christ a single bride, kept by His faithfulness and not by her own. The correspondence is real, but the church is never merely guaranteed a clean record, and Paul still fears for her, 2 Corinthians 11:2 to 3.

Oholibah is made to drink her sister's cup, verses 32 to 34, and the cup is a standing image of God's judgment, Isaiah 51:17. In Gethsemane Jesus prays, 'let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39, and tells Peter to put away his sword, because He must drink the cup the Father has given, John 18:11. The escalation is that the drinker is not the guilty city but the one who had done no wrong, and that He drains what Oholibah could only be forced to swallow. The type breaks at the point of consent: the sisters drink under compulsion, the Son drinks in obedience and love.

typology.type: Babylon and the prostitute, the bride and the city
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel's allegory feeds the book of Revelation. The woman called Babylon the Great, Revelation 17:1 to 5, holds a golden cup full of impurities and has seduced the kings of the earth, and she is judged by the very powers that once served her, Revelation 17:16. Against her stands the bride of the Lamb in fine linen, Revelation 19:7 to 8, whom John also sees as the new Jerusalem, Revelation 21:2. The pattern of a faithless city judged by her lovers and a faithful bride made ready is Ezekiel 23 carried to its end. The correspondence is symbolic and not geographical, and the identity of Babylon in Revelation is a separate question.

study.christ:
The chapter's answer to its own tragedy is not found within it, and that absence is itself a way to Christ. Ezekiel 23 ends with a people reduced to nothing and a warning to others, and the question that hangs over the last verse is whether God can have a faithful people at all. The New Testament says He can, and that He does so by sending a faithful husband.

The marriage frame is the first road. The prophets cast the Lord as a husband to an unfaithful wife, and Paul takes the picture straight to Christ and the church, 'Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word,' Ephesians 5:25 to 26. In Ezekiel the husband is wronged and the wife is stripped. In Ephesians the husband takes the wrongs upon Himself and clothes her. Hosea's marriage already pointed this way, with a prophet who buys back a wife who has been unfaithful, Hosea 3:1 to 3, and Revelation completes the picture with the bride made ready, Revelation 19:7 to 8.

The tent is the second road. The two names turn on whether God's tent is in the woman, and John says that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, John 1:14. In Christ the divine presence is not a place that can be profaned by child sacrifice at the altar and entering the sanctuary the same day, as verses 38 and 39 describe, but a person who remains holy among sinners. The temple He speaks of is His body, John 2:19 to 21.

The cup is the third road. Oholibah must drink to the dregs the cup her sister drank. The Gospels say Jesus prayed that the cup might pass, and then drank it, Matthew 26:39 and John 18:11. What He drank was not the shame of His own sin but the portion due to the unfaithful, so that 'there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus,' Romans 8:1. Hebrews says He 'endured the cross, scorning its shame,' Hebrews 12:2, and the shame of the exposed, stripped bride of Ezekiel is the shame He took, being stripped Himself, Matthew 27:28.

The contrast of the lovers gives the fourth. The sisters were drawn by what they saw: men dressed in splendor and figures in red on a wall. Christ is the one who is not impressive by that kind of sight, Isaiah 53:2, and yet He is truly beautiful in what He does. The bride who runs after sight is won by a love that she did not earn, Romans 5:8.

Caution is needed. The chapter does not forecast Jesus in any verse, and its details of sexual wrongdoing should not be forced into a one-to-one code. The correspondences rest on the shared marriage frame and on the New Testament's own reading of it, and they should be held as such.
study.god:
The chapter speaks of God as a person who can be hurt, and the way it does so is one of the most striking features of the Old Testament's doctrine of God. He says that Oholah 'became Mine' and bore 'sons and daughters' to Him, verse 4. He says He 'saw' the defiling, verse 13, that His soul was wrenched from her, verse 18, and that He will set 'My jealous rage' against her, verse 25. These are the words of a God who has given Himself, not of one who merely holds a rule.

At the same time He is sovereign over the nations who punish. 'I will delegate judgment to them,' verse 24, and 'they will punish you according to their own standards.' The lovers are not independent agents; they do what He has permitted. Yet Ezekiel does not excuse them by that. The same book proclaims judgment on the nations who go too far, and this chapter's verb for how they will behave, in fury and cruelty, is not praised. God uses what He does not approve.

God is just in a way that fits the crime. The sisters pursued the nations, so the nations come to them. They looked for strength abroad, and so their strength is broken by those same foreigners. The cup is theirs because they chose their sister's path, verse 31. The justice is not arbitrary, and God does not ask for more than the law had always named, as the references to adultery and bloodshed, verse 45, show.

The chapter also shows a God who cares about worship. The sin that makes the sentence final is that the sisters slaughtered their children for idols and on the same day entered His sanctuary, verses 38 and 39. The conjoining of the two acts says that worship divided between God and idols is not a lesser form of worship but a defilement of the house He loves.

And He is the God who desires an end to indecency. 'So I will put an end to your indecency,' verse 27, and again at verse 48. The aim of the judgment is a changed people and a land cleansed, and the book that follows moves toward it, Ezekiel 36:24 to 27, where He promises a new heart and a new spirit.

For worship, the chapter tells us that He wants a whole heart, not a share, and that He is moved when we turn from Him. It also tells us not to presume on closeness. To have God's tent in us is a gift that calls for a more careful faithfulness, not a licence.

crossReferences.note: The earlier allegory of a single faithless wife has the same sentence: judged as women who commit adultery and shed blood, handed to her lovers, stripped, and attacked by a mob. Reading the two chapters together shows that Ezekiel is working from a stable legal picture, and that chapter 23 adds a pair of sisters and a more detailed foreign policy.

Jeremiah describes faithless Israel and unfaithful Judah as sisters. Judah saw Israel's divorce and did not fear, and Jeremiah concludes Israel was more righteous than Judah. It is the closest prophetic parallel, and shows that Ezekiel's charge that Oholibah saw and went further was already a theme.

Where Ezekiel ends in judgment on the two sisters, Hosea looks past judgment to a renewed betrothal. The Lord will betroth His people forever in righteousness, justice, love, compassion and faithfulness. It shows the direction the marriage story is moving, from the husband who is wronged to the husband who restores.

Ahaz went to meet the Assyrian king in Damascus and sent home the plan of the altar he saw there, and Uriah built it. This is a concrete example of the defiling with Assyria's idols of verse 7 and 12, a king's trip to a foreign power ending with a foreign altar in God's house.

Hezekiah welcomed envoys from Babylon and showed them all his treasure house and armory. Isaiah later told him that everything would be carried to Babylon, Isaiah 39:5 to 7. The scene is an early courtship in the story that ends with the messengers and the bed of verses 16 and 17.

Jerusalem has drunk the cup of the Lord's fury and drained the goblet to the dregs. It shows the cup of Ezekiel 23:31 to 34 as a standing figure for the portion God hands out, and prepares for Isaiah's turn, where the cup is taken from her hand.

In Gethsemane Jesus asks that the cup pass from Him and then submits to the Father's will. The cup that Oholibah is forced to drain is the same figure for divine judgment, and Jesus' prayer shows that He took it willingly and in her place.

Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her to sanctify and present her to Himself without stain or wrinkle. It is the faithful husband's answer to the two sisters: He does not divorce the bride for what Ezekiel describes but makes her clean at His own cost.

Paul says he promised the Corinthians to one husband, to present them as a pure virgin to Christ, and fears they may be led astray. It shows that the apostles read Ezekiel's picture of spiritual adultery as a live danger to the church, not only a lesson about ancient Judah.

James addresses his readers as adulterous people and says friendship with the world is enmity toward God. It carries the Old Testament's marriage language of idolatry into the church and shows that political and cultural alliance can still be a form of unfaithfulness.

The great prostitute holds a golden cup full of impurities, and her name is Babylon the Great. The woman, the cup and the foreign power all come out of the world of Ezekiel 23, now stretched to the end of history, and her fate matches that of the sisters judged by their former lovers.

The marriage of the Lamb has come and the bride has made herself ready, clothed in fine linen. It is the final answer to the two sisters: a bride who is clean, and who is made so by the Lamb's work and given her garments.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is a marriage story long before it is a courtroom story. Genesis closes with a man and a woman who are 'one flesh,' Genesis 2:24, and the prophets use that picture to describe how God relates to His people. Ezekiel 23 is where the picture is darkest. It answers the question of how a people who were rescued from Egypt and given a land and a Temple could be reduced to a ruin, and the answer is that they kept loving what they had been taken out of.

Looking back, the chapter gathers the whole history of the divided kingdom into one image. Samaria's fall to Assyria, the long dance of Judah with Assyria, Egypt and Babylon, and the exiles of 597 and 586 are told as a single act of unfaithfulness. It also draws on the idols of Egypt of Ezekiel 20, so the allegory covers the whole span from Exodus to exile.

Looking forward, it sets up the book's turn. Chapter 24 brings the siege, and after the fall Ezekiel moves to promise: the new heart and new spirit of 36:24 to 27, the dry bones of 37, and a new temple where the Lord is present, 40 to 48. The tent that had been defiled is replaced by a sanctuary from which the glory does not leave. The bride is not left behind in her disgrace.

The New Testament carries the story to its end. Christ is the husband who comes for the unfaithful and pays the cost, Ephesians 5:25 to 27. The Word becomes flesh and pitches His tent among us, John 1:14. The cup of wrath is drunk by Him, and the bride of Revelation 19 is clothed in clean linen. The counterfeit, Babylon with her golden cup, is judged, Revelation 17 and 18.

In the new creation the marriage is complete. John sees 'the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband,' Revelation 21:2, and hears that 'the dwelling place of God is with man,' verse 3. The tent that Oholibah's name proclaimed, and that she could not keep faith with, is now with His people, and there is no temple in the city, because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. Unfaithfulness is not simply forgiven but ended, and the sisters' history is finished in a bride who is never again led astray.

sermon.title: No Fidelity Without Remembering (Ezek. 16; 23)
sermon.why: Carson's message works through both Ezekiel 16 and 23 together, directly addressing this chapter's picture of Oholah and Oholibah as a second, intensified allegory of Israel and Judah's covenant unfaithfulness, and lands on the same call to remember God's covenant faithfulness despite repeated betrayal that this study follows.

quiz.q: What do the names Oholah and Oholibah represent, and what wordplay do they contain?

options.text: Samaria and Jerusalem, with names playing on the Hebrew word for 'tent,' Jerusalem's name marking her as the city where God's true tent, the temple, stood.
options.note: Verse 4 identifies the sisters directly, and the names' wordplay on 'tent' underlies why Jerusalem's guilt is judged as greater.

options.text: Two entirely fictional cities with no historical referent.
options.note: Verse 4 explicitly identifies them as Samaria and Jerusalem, real historical cities.

options.text: Egypt and Assyria, the two foreign powers named in the allegory.
options.note: Egypt and Assyria are the lovers pursued in the allegory, not the two sisters themselves.

options.text: Two unrelated tribes with no shared origin.
options.note: Verse 2 specifically calls them 'daughters of the same mother,' emphasizing their shared origin, not an unrelated status.

quiz.q: According to verse 11, how does Oholibah's unfaithfulness compare to her sister's?

options.text: She was less depraved than her sister, having learned from Oholah's example.
options.note: Verse 11 states the opposite: she was more depraved than her sister, not less.

options.text: She was more depraved in her lust and prostitution than her sister.
options.note: Verse 11 states this directly: 'in her lust and prostitution she was more depraved than her sister.'

options.text: She was equally unfaithful, with no difference noted between the sisters.
options.note: The text specifically ranks Oholibah's guilt as exceeding her sister's, not merely equal.

options.text: She remained faithful while only her sister was unfaithful.
options.note: Verse 11 describes Oholibah's own unfaithfulness directly, not faithfulness.

quiz.q: Who ultimately executes judgment against Oholibah, according to verses 22-24?

options.text: A coalition of angels sent directly from heaven.
options.note: The judgment is carried out by human armies, the very nations she once pursued as lovers, not angelic beings.

options.text: Egypt alone, acting in isolation from other nations.
options.note: The judgment involves Babylonians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians together, not Egypt acting alone.

options.text: The very lovers she once pursued and then turned from in disgust, incited by God against her.
options.note: Verses 22-24 describe God inciting her former lovers, Babylonians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians, against her.

options.text: No one; the judgment described never actually takes place in the text.
options.note: The judgment is described as certain and detailed, not left unfulfilled or hypothetical.

quiz.q: What shared abomination involving children is named in verses 37-39?

options.text: Neglecting to educate their children in the law.
options.note: The abomination named is far graver, the sacrifice of children in fire, not educational neglect.

options.text: Sacrificing their children in the fire to idols, even entering God's sanctuary to profane it on the same day.
options.note: Verses 37-39 state this explicitly, naming both the child sacrifice and the same-day defiling of the sanctuary.

options.text: Sending their children away as required tribute to foreign powers.
options.note: The text describes child sacrifice to idols specifically, not the payment of children as political tribute.

options.text: Refusing to have children as an act of protest.
options.note: The passage describes the opposite issue, bearing children to God and then sacrificing them, not childlessness.

quiz.q: What is the stated purpose of the sentence carried out in the chapter's closing verses, 43-49?

options.text: To reward the sisters for their political alliances.
options.note: The passage describes judgment and punishment, not reward, for the sisters' behavior.

options.text: To put an end to indecency in the land and warn all women not to imitate this behavior.
options.note: Verse 48 states this purpose directly: 'I will put an end to indecency in the land, and all the women will be admonished not to imitate your behavior.'

options.text: To restore both sisters immediately to their former royal privileges.
options.note: The passage describes judgment being carried out, not an immediate restoration of privilege.

options.text: To have no lasting effect on future behavior at all.
options.note: The stated purpose is explicitly corrective and preventive, meant to end this pattern, not to be inconsequential.

questions: Jerusalem's greater privilege, God's own dwelling within her, became the measure of her greater guilt when she was unfaithful. Where has God given you particular closeness or blessing that carries with it a greater responsibility you may be neglecting?

Both sisters pursued powerful political alliances as a substitute for trusting God alone. What 'alliances,' whether relationships, achievements, or security measures, are you tempted to lean on instead of trusting God?
The very nations Oholibah once desired became the instruments of her judgment. Have you ever seen something you pursued as a source of security or pleasure turn out to bring you harm instead?

This chapter names God's own grief, disgust, and jealousy at betrayal in strikingly personal terms. How does it change your view of sin to see it primarily as a wound to a relationship with God rather than merely breaking an abstract rule?

Where Jerusalem repeatedly failed to remain faithful despite every privilege, Christ remains faithful to His unfaithful people and cleanses them fully. Where do you need to rest in Christ's faithfulness rather than your own record of faithfulness to Him?

translationNotes.note: The names Oholah and Oholibah are both built from the Hebrew word 'ohel,' tent, a deliberate wordplay likely alluding to the tabernacle and later temple, marking Jerusalem's name as claiming God's own tent uniquely 'in her,' which the allegory uses to explain her graver guilt.

'Pekod, Shoa, and Koa' are place names associated with Babylonian provinces or peoples, mentioned also in Jeremiah 50:21; their inclusion underscores the comprehensive, coalition nature of the judgment brought against Oholibah.

The image of drinking a 'cup' of judgment is a common prophetic metaphor, Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15-29, picturing divine wrath as an intoxicating drink whose effects, staggering, shame, and collapse, are unavoidable once poured out.
